past_medical_history: Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis with previous laminectomy
Prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy at 72, in remission
family_history: Father died of myocardial infarction at 70

social_history.living_situation: Lives with his daughter; she attends and manages his medication

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, year correct, month incorrect. MoCA 18/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, clock, digit span, serial sevens, fluency (7 animals) and delayed recall (1/5 unaided, 1/5 with cueing, 2/5 recognition).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech fluent with word-finding pauses.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk with mild distal wasting in the legs. Tone normal. Strength 5/5 proximally, 4+/5 ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally, attributed to the lumbar stenosis.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced vibration at the ankles with a patchy L5-S1 distribution of sensory loss, long-standing.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ knees, absent ankle jerks, plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.gait: Stooped and cautious with reduced step length, limited by neurogenic claudication after 200 metres; arm swing preserved. Uses a stick.
neurological_exam.additional: Pulse irregularly irregular at 78. No frontal release signs. No parkinsonian features.

patient.chief_complaint: Three years of gradually worsening memory, with the family asking whether it is his heart or his brain
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Alberto Riva is an 81-year-old retired notary clerk who attends with his daughter. She describes three years of gradual decline, memory first: he forgets conversations within the hour, has lost the thread of the family finances he used to keep, and now needs prompting to take medication. There have been no abrupt steps she can date and no episodes of weakness or speech loss. In the last year he has begun to lose words. He has had atrial fibrillation for six years and has been reliably anticoagulated on edoxaban. His daughter's specific question is whether the atrial fibrillation is 'causing small strokes'. He also has lumbar stenosis with neurogenic claudication and long-standing numb feet, and a laminectomy eight years ago. He declines a lumbar puncture when it is offered, both because of the previous spinal surgery and because he is anticoagulated. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. His blood pressure runs at 150 systolic.

signal_characteristics.Coronal_T1: Reduced hippocampal height with widened choroidal and hippocampal fissures bilaterally

signal_characteristics.T1: Sulcal widening in the temporoparietal convexities beyond that expected for 81 years

findings.type: White matter hyperintensity of presumed vascular origin

findings.location: Left corona radiata, right thalamus, left putamen

signal_characteristics.SWI: Deep distribution; no lobar microbleeds and no cortical superficial siderosis

volumetrics.medial_temporal_atrophy: Scheltens MTA grade 3 bilaterally — beyond the age-adjusted range even at 81
volumetrics.ventricular_system: Evans index 0.30 with disproportionate temporal horn enlargement

additional_observations: Marked medial temporal atrophy with temporoparietal cortical loss, plus a Fazekas 2 small-vessel burden with three lacunes and two deep microbleeds
No cortical or territorial infarct after six years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation
Microbleeds are strictly deep — hypertensive rather than amyloid angiopathy — which matters for the anticoagulation decision
mri.impression: Two processes: Alzheimer-type medial temporal and temporoparietal atrophy, and moderate hypertensive small-vessel disease with three lacunes and two deep microbleeds. No embolic infarct despite long-standing atrial fibrillation.

labs.interpretation: LDL 104 mg/dL is above target. Renal function is impaired at eGFR 52, relevant to anticoagulant dosing. TSH, B12, folate, RPR and HIV are normal or negative. There is no reversible cause.

findings.region: Prefrontal, precuneus and lateral temporoparietal cortex
findings.signal: Diffuse bilateral cortical binding with loss of the grey-white boundary; SUVr 1.48 against a positivity threshold of 1.11

advanced_imaging.impression: Positive amyloid PET with a typical Alzheimer distribution. Amyloid pathology is established. Combined with the small-vessel burden on MRI, the diagnosis is mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia.

quantitative_data.pattern: storage-type amnesia with executive and naming involvement

specialized_test.impression: Storage-type amnesia with impaired recognition, reduced naming and a dysexecutive component. The amnestic core is degenerative; the executive slowing is compatible with the vascular burden.

findings.performance: 1/5 unaided, no cue benefit, 2/5 recognition — storage-type deficit

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 18/30 with a storage-type amnesia that gains nothing from cueing, plus language, executive and visuospatial involvement. The gradual amnestic-led course points to Alzheimer pathology; the vascular burden on imaging is the second question.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia — amyloid-PET-confirmed Alzheimer pathology with moderate hypertensive small-vessel disease

differential.key_features: The amnestic profile, Scheltens 3 atrophy and a positive amyloid PET establish Alzheimer pathology; the additional Fazekas 2 burden with three lacunes is a real second contributor whose risk factors are treatable
Six years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation with no cortical or territorial infarct on MRI — the family's hypothesis is reasonable and the imaging refutes it
A storage-type amnesia unresponsive to cueing with Scheltens 3 atrophy is not produced by a Fazekas 2 burden

Evans index 0.30 with disproportionate temporal horn enlargement is the atrophy pattern, the gait is limited by neurogenic claudication rather than magnetic, and there is no disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space

differential.diagnosis: Cervical or lumbar myelopathy contributing to the gait
differential.key_features: The lumbar stenosis and radiculopathy explain the leg findings and the claudication but have no bearing on cognition

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Three years of gradual amnestic-led decline with no dateable steps in a patient with well-anticoagulated atrial fibrillation, plus a long-standing lumbar radicular problem accounting for the leg findings

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 18/30 with a storage-type amnesia unresponsive to cueing and multi-domain involvement, on a gradual course

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; LDL above target and eGFR 52 relevant to anticoagulant dosing

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Scheltens 3 medial temporal atrophy with temporoparietal loss plus a Fazekas 2 burden with three lacunes and two strictly deep microbleeds, and no embolic infarct

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amnestic-led multi-domain profile with impaired recognition — Alzheimer-type storage failure with a vascular executive overlay

optimal_actions.action: Obtain amyloid PET where coexisting Alzheimer pathology is the specific question and CSF sampling is declined or unavailable
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention — Alzheimer pathology is established without a lumbar puncture, which the patient declined and which his anticoagulation and previous spinal surgery made unattractive

optimal_actions.action: Obtain FDG-PET to separate a temporoparietal Alzheimer pattern from the patchy multifocal hypometabolism that follows white matter lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism with additional patchy frontal defects — both processes visible on one study

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Establish Alzheimer pathology without a lumbar puncture in a patient who declined it and is anticoagulated after spinal surgery, start a cholinesterase inhibitor, continue edoxaban with renal-appropriate dosing since the microbleeds are deep and there are no falls, bring blood pressure below 130 mmHg systolic and LDL below 70 mg/dL, and provide medication supervision and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Alzheimer pathology established by amyloid PET rather than lumbar puncture, symptomatic therapy started, anticoagulation continued with renal dose review, and vascular targets set

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Characterise the amnesia as storage or retrieval type
Read the MRI for both the atrophy grade and the vascular burden, and note the absence of embolic infarction
Answer the family's question about atrial fibrillation directly with the imaging evidence
Choose a biomarker route the patient will accept: amyloid PET where lumbar puncture is declined, anticoagulation is in place and there has been spinal surgery
Exclude reversible causes and review renal function for anticoagulant dosing
Name mixed disease and treat both components
Separate the lumbar radicular findings from the neurological attribution
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform a lumbar puncture in an anticoagulated patient who has declined it when a non-invasive biomarker will answer the same question
Do not stop anticoagulation for two strictly deep microbleeds in a patient with atrial fibrillation and no falls
Do not attribute the dementia to atrial fibrillation when there is no infarct on MRI
Do not prescribe anticholinergic bladder agents alongside a cholinesterase inhibitor
Do not attribute the gait disturbance to the dementia when neurogenic claudication and absent ankle jerks explain it
key_reasoning_points: Amyloid PET and CSF answer the same question, and the choice between them is a patient-level decision: anticoagulation, previous spinal surgery and a declined procedure all point away from a lumbar puncture here
Absence of cortical infarction after six years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation is evidence that the arrhythmia is not the mechanism, and it answers the family's question with data
Microbleed distribution decides the anticoagulation question: strictly deep means hypertensive arteriopathy and does not overturn the indication, whereas lobar microbleeds with siderosis would
A coexisting spinal problem can account for gait and reflex findings without contributing anything to the cognitive diagnosis, and conflating them wastes investigation
Naming mixed disease produces two treatment plans; naming one leaves the other untreated

red_herrings.data_point: Six years of atrial fibrillation and a family convinced it is causing small strokes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Directs the workup to embolic sources and prolonged monitoring, and away from the degenerative diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: There is no cortical or territorial infarct on MRI after six years of effective anticoagulation; the mechanism is degenerative with a small-vessel contribution

red_herrings.data_point: Absent ankle jerks with distal sensory loss and a stooped gait
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a neurological cause for the gait that belongs to the dementia syndrome, or prompts a workup for polyneuropathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The findings are radicular and date to long-standing lumbar stenosis with a previous laminectomy; they are unrelated to the cognitive diagnosis

key_educational_points: Amyloid PET and CSF biomarkers are interchangeable in what they answer, and the choice is made on patient-level factors
The absence of infarction on MRI is what refutes a cardioembolic attribution, however long the arrhythmia has been present
Deep microbleeds do not contraindicate anticoagulation; lobar microbleeds with siderosis are a different matter
Coexisting spinal disease explains leg findings without contributing to a cognitive diagnosis
